newsitem.title: UK: British gun owners angered by proposed handgun ban.
newsitem.headline: British gun owners angered by proposed handgun ban.

text.p: Britain's private gun owners reacted angrily on Thursday to government plans to outlaw most handguns in the aftermath of the murder of 16 children and their teacher at a Scottish primary school last March.

The regulations, said by the government to be among the toughest in the world, are expected to become law by Christmas. They will ban 80 percent of the country's 200,000 legally-held handguns except single-shot, .22-inch calibre weapons.
Stricter security measures will mean that the smaller calibre guns, which are widely used in shooting competitions, must be securely locked away in guns clubs.

"This is the behaviour of a Third World dictatorship rather than a Western democracy," complained Richard Law, secretary of the Shooter's Rights Association. "The plans are not practical or relevant."

More defiant talk came from Alex Boyd, secretary of a gun club in Scotland which refused membership to Thomas Hamilton membership just weeks before he rampaged through Dunblane primary school murdering the children and their teacher.

Boyd said he would fight the ban and take the case to a European court if necessary. "Picking on gun clubs is the easy way out. Blame us and everyone's happy -- well it is not good enough. We are not going to let them get away with it."

In addition to the ban, all gun clubs will need a licence and must have stricter standards and alarms linked to police stations. All handgun shooters must have firearms certificates and police will be able to exchange information about owners.
The government proposals went beyond what was recommended by Lord Douglas Cullen, a senior judge who conducted an inquiry into the Dunblane tragedy.
But opposition politicans, the parents of the dead children and some British newspapers called for a complete ban.
"Dunblane betrayed," screamed The Sun, the country's top selling newspaper, in a banner front-page headline. "This government is willing to tolerate another massacre."
Its main rival, The Daily Mirror, echoed the sentiment and urged Prime Minister John Major to ban all handguns.

Dr Mick North, who was treating wounded children in a local hospital when he learned his own daughter Sophie was one of those killed, promised that the parents would continue their campaign to get all handguns out of private hands.
"The government should take one step further and ban all handguns. We think the government must take account of public feeling. Our campaign will continue," he said.

Major, with a majority of just two in the 651-seat lower House of Commons, was advised that he risked defeat in parliament via a revolt by members of his ruling Conservative party unless he went much further.
Demanding a free vote, former minister David Mellor said: "It is time to conclude that, literally and metaphorically, the game is up for handguns now. That is the public will."
But gun shops and clubs throughout Britain said even the compromise measures which the government proposed would put them out of business and ruin a sport celebrated at the Olympics.

"For a political point the government is destroying a sport which millions enjoy, yet they will not make a noticeable difference to public safety with these measures," argued Christopher Reader, secretary of another rifle and pistol club.

The government says the ban is expected to cost an estimated 24 million pounds ($38 million) in compensation for recovered weapons. The Shooters' Rights Association say this is a gross underestimate and the real figure could be closer to 1 billion pounds ($1.6 billion).

"I have got children myself and it is a terrible thing that happened in Dunblane but you are not going to get those kids back by punishing 50,000 to 60,000 people like me who are law- abiding citizens," one gun enthusiast said.
